paragraphs.heading: What Pangaea was
paragraphs.text: Pangaea was a supercontinent of the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic eras. It was shaped like a letter C, with most of its mass stretching between the northern and southern polar regions of the Earth. Around it lay the superocean Panthalassa, along with the Paleo-Tethys and later the Tethys Oceans. No supercontinent has existed more recently, and Pangaea was the first one that geologists reconstructed.

paragraphs.heading: A name and an idea
paragraphs.text: The name comes from Ancient Greek: pan, meaning all or whole, and Gaia, meaning Mother Earth or land. Abraham Ortelius may have been the first to suggest, in 1596, that the continents were once joined and later separated. Alfred Wegener, who originated the scientific theory of continental drift, put forward the idea of one joined landmass, with supporting evidence, in three journal articles in 1912. In a 1915 book he proposed that all the continents had formed one supercontinent before breaking up and drifting to where they are now. He called it the Urkontinent, and used the name "Pangaea" just once, in the 1920 edition of the book.

paragraphs.heading: Why acceptance was slow
paragraphs.text: Wegener first proposed that Pangaea broke up because centrifugal forces from the Earth's rotation acted on the high continents. That mechanism was easily shown to be physically implausible, and this delayed acceptance of the Pangaea hypothesis. Arthur Holmes proposed a more plausible mechanism, mantle convection. Combined with evidence from mapping the ocean floor after the Second World War, it led to plate tectonics being developed and accepted as a theory. That theory gives the widely accepted explanation for why Pangaea existed and why it broke apart.

paragraphs.heading: Clues in coastlines and rocks
paragraphs.text: The first evidence came from the geography of the continents that border the Atlantic Ocean. People remarked on how closely the coasts of North and South America seemed to fit those of Europe and Africa almost as soon as the coasts were charted. Careful reconstructions showed a mismatch of less than 130 km at the 500 fathoms (910 meters) contour, which was argued to be far too similar to be coincidence. Geological trends also match across three coasts: eastern South America, eastern North America and western Africa. Glacial deposits of the same age and structure turn up on many continents that are separate now but would have been together in Pangaea.

paragraphs.heading: Clues in fossils
paragraphs.text: Fossils point the same way: similar and even identical species are found on continents that are now great distances apart. Lystrosaurus fossils turn up in South Africa, India and Antarctica, together with members of the Glossopteris flora. With the continents in their present positions, the distribution of that flora would have reached from the polar circle to the equator. Mesosaurus, a freshwater reptile, has been found only in limited areas on the coasts of Brazil and West Africa.

paragraphs.heading: Reading old magnetism
paragraphs.text: Geologists can also work out how continental plates moved by looking at the orientation of magnetic minerals in rocks. A rock takes on the Earth's magnetic orientation when it forms, which shows the direction of the poles relative to that rock. This gives latitudes and orientations, though not longitudes. Rock samples whose ages differ by millions of years show magnetic differences, caused by a combination of magnetic polar wander and the drifting of continents. The polar wander part, which is the same for all samples of one age, can be subtracted, leaving the part that shows continental drift.

paragraphs.heading: Not the only supercontinent
paragraphs.text: Supercontinents appear to form and break up in a cycle through Earth's history, and there may have been several before Pangaea. One, Rodinia, existed from roughly 1.3 billion to about 750 million years ago. A later one, Pannotia, was relatively short-lived and lasted until 540 million years ago, near the start of the Cambrian. When Pannotia broke up it gave rise to the continents of Laurentia and Baltica and to the southern supercontinent Gondwana. Reconstructions of continents from before Pangaea remain partly speculative, and different ones differ in some details.
